q: Work is done on a body by a force only when:
o: The force acts on the body, whether or not the body moves
The body moves at constant velocity with no force acting on it
The force always acts at right angles to the motion
The body is displaced and the displacement has a component along the force
x: W = Fd cos θ, so work needs a displacement with a component along the force. A force with no displacement, or one at 90° to the motion, does no work.

q: A force vector F = (3i + 4j) N moves a body through a displacement vector d = (2i + j) m. The work done is:
x: W = F·d = (3)(2) + (4)(1) = 6 + 4 = 10 J. Work is the scalar product, so matching components are multiplied and added.

q: A 3 kg stone is tossed straight up and climbs 4 m before stopping. How much work does gravity do on it during this climb? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
x: Gravity (30 N) acts downward while the stone moves 4 m upward, so θ = 180° and W = 30 × 4 × cos 180° = −120 J.

q: A block slides down a fixed smooth inclined plane. The work done on the block by the normal reaction of the plane is:
o: Positive, because the block speeds up
Zero, because the normal force is perpendicular to the displacement
Negative, because the normal force opposes gravity
Equal to the loss of potential energy of the block
x: The normal reaction acts at 90° to the surface, and the block moves along the surface, so cos 90° = 0 and the work is zero. The speeding up is due to gravity.

q: The work done by a constant force on a moving body is negative when the angle θ between the force and the displacement lies in the range:
x: W = Fd cos θ is negative when cos θ is negative, i.e. for angles greater than 90° up to 180°. At exactly 90° the work is zero.

q: A porter holds a 20 kg suitcase still above the ground for 5 minutes and feels tired. The work he does on the suitcase is:
o: Zero, because the suitcase has no displacement
x: Work needs displacement. The suitcase does not move, so no work is done on it; the tiredness is due to energy used inside his muscles.

q: A 6 kg block is pulled 4 m up a smooth incline that makes 30° with the horizontal, at constant speed, by a force parallel to the incline. The work done by this force is (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 30° = 0.5):
x: At constant speed on a smooth incline the pull equals mg sin 30° = 60 × 0.5 = 30 N. W = 30 × 4 = 120 J. Using mg × 4 = 240 J forgets the sine factor.

q: The energy stored in food and fuels such as petrol and coal is:
x: Food and fuels store energy in chemical bonds; it is released as heat and work when they react, for example during burning or respiration.

q: When a torch is switched on, the main energy changes taking place are:
o: Chemical energy of the cells → electrical energy → light and heat
x: The cells convert stored chemical energy into electrical energy, which the bulb converts into light and some heat.

q: One electron-volt (eV), a unit used for very small energies, is equal to:
x: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V: (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1 V) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. 3.6 × 10⁶ J is one kilowatt-hour.

q: A simple pendulum swings with no air resistance. At the lowest point of its swing the bob has:
o: Maximum potential energy and zero kinetic energy
Zero kinetic energy and zero potential energy
Maximum kinetic energy and minimum potential energy
x: As the bob falls to its lowest point, potential energy turns into kinetic energy, so its speed and kinetic energy are greatest there; the total energy stays constant.

q: A 100 W bulb is left on for 10 hours. The electrical energy it uses is:
x: Energy = power × time = 0.1 kW × 10 h = 1 kWh. Using 100 instead of 0.1 kW gives the 1000 kWh error.

q: In a solar cell, the main energy change is from:
x: A solar (photovoltaic) cell absorbs light and produces an electric current, so it converts light energy into electrical energy.

q: A 0.5 kg ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, at what height above the point of projection are its kinetic and potential energies equal? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
x: Total energy = ½ × 0.5 × 20² = 100 J. When KE = PE, PE = 50 J, so h = 50 ÷ (0.5 × 10) = 10 m, half the maximum height of 20 m.

q: Kinetic energy is the energy a body possesses because of its:
x: Kinetic energy is energy due to motion, ½mv². Energy due to position or shape is potential energy.

q: A 4 kg body has 50 J of kinetic energy. Its speed is:
x: ½ × 4 × v² = 50, so v² = 25 and v = 5 m s⁻¹. 25 m s⁻¹ forgets to take the square root.

q: The mass of a body is halved and its speed is doubled. Its kinetic energy becomes:
x: KE = ½mv². Halving m gives ×½ and doubling v gives ×4, so KE becomes ½ × 4 = 2 times.

q: A 2 kg body has a linear momentum of 10 kg m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy is:
x: KE = p²/2m = 100 ÷ 4 = 25 J. Using p²/m gives 50 J, which forgets the factor 2.

q: How much work must be done on a 3 kg trolley on a smooth level floor to increase its speed from 2 m s⁻¹ to 4 m s⁻¹?
x: Work = change in KE = ½ × 3 × (4² − 2²) = 1.5 × 12 = 18 J. Squaring the change in speed, ½ × 3 × 2², gives the wrong 6 J.

q: Body X has the same linear momentum as body Y, but X has only half the mass of Y. KE of X : KE of Y is:
x: With equal momentum, KE = p²/2m is inversely proportional to mass, so X, with half the mass, has twice the kinetic energy of Y.

q: A 10 g bullet moving at 200 m s⁻¹ penetrates 0.1 m into a wooden block and stops. The average resistive force of the wood is:
x: KE = ½ × 0.01 × 200² = 200 J. This is used up as work against the wood: F × 0.1 = 200, so F = 2000 N.

q: Near the Earth's surface, the gravitational potential energy of a body of mass m at height h is:
x: Lifting a body of weight mg through height h needs work mgh, which is stored as gravitational potential energy.

q: When a body is lifted at constant speed, the work done against gravity is stored in the body as:
x: At constant speed the kinetic energy does not change, so the work done against gravity is stored as gravitational potential energy.

q: A box of mass m is lifted to the same height h once slowly and once quickly. The gravitational potential energy gained is:
o: The same, mgh, in both cases
x: Gravitational PE depends only on mass, g and height. The time taken affects the power needed, not the potential energy gained.

q: A 60 kg person climbs a staircase and gains 18 kJ of gravitational potential energy. The height climbed is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: h = PE ÷ mg = 18 000 ÷ 600 = 30 m. Forgetting the 'kilo' in 18 kJ gives 0.03 m, and dividing by m only gives 300 m.

q: If both the mass of a body and its height above the ground are doubled, its gravitational potential energy becomes:
x: PE = mgh is proportional to both m and h, so doubling each gives 2 × 2 = 4 times.

q: A body is raised through the same height on the Moon (g about one-sixth of Earth's) as on the Earth. The gravitational potential energy it gains on the Moon is:
o: Six times that on the Earth
The same as on the Earth
Zero, because the Moon has no air
One-sixth of that on the Earth
x: PE = mgh and the mass and height are the same, so the PE is proportional to g: one-sixth of the Earth value. Air has nothing to do with it.

q: A 2 kg box is lifted vertically through 5 m and then carried 10 m horizontally at that height. The total gain in its gravitational potential energy is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Only the vertical rise changes gravitational PE: 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. The horizontal movement is perpendicular to gravity, so it adds nothing.

q: A table top is taken as the zero level. A book resting on a shelf higher than the table top has a potential energy that is:
o: Always equal to its kinetic energy
x: PE = mgh with h measured from the zero level. The book is above the table top, so h and PE are positive; below the table top PE would be negative.

q: A 3 kg lamp hangs 3 m below a ceiling. If the ceiling is taken as the reference level, the gravitational potential energy of the lamp is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: The lamp is 3 m below the reference level, so h = −3 m and PE = 3 × 10 × (−3) = −90 J.

q: A 1 kg stone rests at the bottom of a well 10 m deep. Taking ground level as zero, the potential energy of the stone is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: The stone is 10 m below the reference level: PE = 1 × 10 × (−10) = −100 J. −10 J forgets to multiply by g.

q: A body has a gravitational potential energy of −50 J relative to a chosen reference level. This means that:
o: It has 50 J less mass than at the reference level
It will rise by itself to the reference level
50 J of work must be done on it to raise it to the reference level
x: Negative PE means the body is below the reference level, so 50 J of work against gravity is needed to lift it up to the zero level.

q: Taking the ground as zero, a 1 kg bucket in a well is lowered from a depth of 2 m to a depth of 4 m. Its potential energy changes by (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: PE changes from −20 J to −40 J, so ΔPE = −40 − (−20) = −20 J. The bucket went down, so its PE decreased.

q: Two students use different reference levels to work out the gravitational potential energy of the same falling ball. Which quantity will they both find the same?
o: The potential energy of the ball at its starting point
The sign of the potential energy at the floor
The potential energy of the ball at the floor
The work done by gravity as the ball falls between two given points
x: The value and sign of PE at a point depend on the reference level, but the work done by gravity (the change in PE) between two points does not.

q: Taking zero potential energy at infinity, the gravitational potential energy of a satellite at a distance 2R from the Earth's centre (R = Earth's radius) compared with its value at the Earth's surface is:
o: Half in magnitude, and still negative
Twice in magnitude, and still negative
x: Absolute PE = −GMm/r. At r = 2R it is −GMm/2R, half the surface value −GMm/R in magnitude, so it is greater (less negative) than at the surface. It is still negative; it only reaches zero at infinity.

q: One watt is equal to:
x: Power is the rate of doing work, so 1 watt is 1 joule of work done per second.

q: A force acts on a moving body at right angles to its velocity at every instant. The power delivered by this force is:
x: P = F·v = Fv cos θ. With θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so the force delivers no power and does no work.

q: A tractor's engine delivers 20 kW while it pulls a trailer with a force of 4000 N in the direction of motion. The speed of the tractor is:
x: P = Fv, so v = 20 000 ÷ 4000 = 5 m s⁻¹. Dividing the force by the power instead gives the wrong 0.2.

q: A boy does 600 J of work in 2 minutes. His average power is:
x: P = W/t = 600 ÷ 120 s = 5 W. Using 2 instead of 120 s gives the wrong answer of 300 W.

q: The kilowatt-hour, printed on electricity bills, is a unit of:
x: A kilowatt-hour is power multiplied by time (1 kW for 1 h), so it is a unit of energy, equal to 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

q: A force vector F = (2i + 3j) N acts on a body moving with velocity vector v = (4i − 2j) m s⁻¹. The power delivered by the force is:
x: P = F·v = (2)(4) + (3)(−2) = 8 − 6 = 2 W. Adding magnitudes of the products (8 + 6) gives the wrong 14 W.

q: A 1200 kg car climbs a straight road at a constant 10 m s⁻¹. The road rises 1 m for every 20 m along it (sin θ = 1/20). Ignoring friction, the power needed is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Force needed = mg sin θ = 12 000 × 1/20 = 600 N. P = Fv = 600 × 10 = 6000 W = 6 kW. Using mg v without sin θ gives 120 kW.

q: When the brakes of a moving car are applied and it stops, its kinetic energy is mainly converted into:
o: Heat in the brakes and tyres
x: The brakes stop the car by friction. The work done against friction changes the kinetic energy into heat in the brake parts, tyres and road.

q: A 5 kg box is pushed 6 m at constant speed across a level floor. The coefficient of friction is 0.2. The heat produced by friction is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Friction = μmg = 0.2 × 5 × 10 = 10 N. Heat = work against friction = 10 × 6 = 60 J. Using mg × d = 300 J forgets μ.

q: A sledge comes down a rough snowy hillside without speeding up. Where does the gravitational potential energy it loses go?
o: All of it becomes kinetic energy of the sledge
All of it is dissipated as heat through work done against friction
It is stored as elastic energy in the snow
It becomes extra potential energy at the bottom
x: At constant speed the kinetic energy does not change, so all the gravitational PE lost is used up as work against friction and appears as heat.

q: A drill bit becomes very hot while drilling a hole in a wall. The main reason is that:
o: Electrical energy flows directly into the bit as heat
The wall gives its own heat to the drill bit
The bit gains gravitational potential energy
Work done against friction is converted into internal energy
x: The bit rubs against the wall material; the work done against friction raises the internal energy of the bit and wall, so they get hot.

q: Two identical blocks are released from the same height, one down a smooth slope and one down a rough slope. At the bottom, the block on the rough slope has:
o: More kinetic energy, because friction pushes it along
Less kinetic energy, the difference being the work done against friction
The same kinetic energy as the other block
Zero kinetic energy in every case
x: Both lose the same PE. On the rough slope part of it is dissipated as heat by friction, so less is left as kinetic energy.

q: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is braked to rest on a level road. Ignoring other losses, the heat produced in the brakes is:
x: Heat = KE lost = ½ × 1000 × 20² = 2 × 10⁵ J. Forgetting the ½ gives 4 × 10⁵ J; forgetting to square gives 1 × 10⁴ J.

q: A 2 kg block is released from rest at the top of a rough slope 5 m high and reaches the bottom at 8 m s⁻¹. The energy dissipated as heat by friction is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: PE lost = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. KE gained = ½ × 2 × 8² = 64 J. Energy lost to friction = 100 − 64 = 36 J.

q: An ideal machine, in which no energy is wasted, would have an efficiency of:
x: If no energy is wasted, all the input becomes useful output, so efficiency = 100%. Real machines always fall short of this.

q: A filament lamp takes in 60 J of electrical energy every second and its efficiency as a light source is 20%. The light energy it gives out each second is:
x: Useful output = 20% of 60 J = 12 J of light; the other 48 J becomes heat. 48 J is the wasted part, not the useful output.

q: An engine wastes 300 J out of every 1000 J of energy it takes in. Its efficiency is:
x: Useful output = 1000 − 300 = 700 J. Efficiency = 700 ÷ 1000 × 100% = 70%. 30% is the fraction wasted.

q: In most practical machines and devices, the energy that is wasted finally ends up mainly as:
o: Thermal energy spread into the surroundings
Extra kinetic energy of the machine
Gravitational potential energy of the parts
x: Losses come mainly from friction, resistance and vibration, which all end up as heat that spreads into the surroundings and cannot easily be used again.

q: An LED bulb and a filament bulb give the same amount of light, but the LED uses much less electrical power. This is because the LED:
o: Wastes less energy as heat, so it is more efficient
Produces more heat than the filament bulb
Does not obey the law of conservation of energy
Stores the extra energy inside it
x: Both give the same useful light output, but the filament bulb turns most of its input into heat. The LED wastes less, so its efficiency is higher.

q: Besides energies, the efficiency of a device can also be calculated as:
x: Power is energy per unit time, so for the same time interval the ratio of output to input power equals the ratio of output to input energy.

q: A hoist with an efficiency of 50% raises a 20 kg crate 5 m in 4 s at constant speed. What electrical power must be supplied to it? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
x: Useful power = mgh/t = 20 × 10 × 5 ÷ 4 = 250 W. Input power = 250 ÷ 0.5 = 500 W. 125 W wrongly multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing.
